SoftGym: Benchmarking Deep Reinforcement Learning for Deformable Object Manipulation

Ten simulated cloth, rope and fluid manipulation tasks built on Nvidia's FleX particle simulator, benchmarked with a standard OpenAI Gym API — image-based RL plateaus far below optimal performance on three of the six tasks (StraightenRope, SpreadCloth, FoldCloth), and closes much more of the gap on the rest.

// the gap

What problem is this solving?

By 2020, deep RL had a standard testbed for almost every kind of rigid manipulation — the Arcade Learning Environment, MuJoCo/DeepMind Control Suite, Meta-World, RLBench, SURREAL — but nothing standard for deformable objects: cloth, rope, fluid. That's not a small gap. Folding laundry, packaging food, handling cables and pouring liquids are exactly the manipulation tasks robots still can't do reliably, and the paper is blunt about why prior work can't be compared: existing papers on deformable manipulation "each evaluate on a different task variant with different simulators or robot setups, making it challenging to directly compare these approaches." Every group builds its own cloth simulator, its own reward function, its own success criterion, and then reports a number that means nothing outside that one paper.

The deeper reason no shared benchmark existed is that deformable objects break the assumption almost every existing RL benchmark quietly relies on: a low-dimensional, directly-observable state. A rigid robot arm's state is a handful of joint angles and velocities. A piece of cloth's state, if you want to fully describe it, is the position of every particle on its surface — "hundreds to thousands" of dimensions in this paper's own simulator, and one that can't be read off a real robot's proprioception the way joint angles can. So a benchmark for this domain has to confront, head-on, two things rigid-body benchmarks get to sidestep: a state space with an inherently high intrinsic dimensionality, and partial observability, since a real system only ever gets images or other indirect sensing of that state, never the particle positions themselves. SoftGym is built specifically to make that confrontation measurable, rather than staying an implicit difficulty everyone works around differently.

// how it works

The method

SoftGym is a set of open-source simulated environments built on top of Nvidia's FleX, a particle- and position-based physics engine: every object — rope, cloth, fluid — is represented as a set of particles connected by constraints (stretching and bending springs for cloth, incompressibility constraints for fluid), and the simulator resolves those constraints each step to advance particle positions and velocities. Wrapping this in a standard OpenAI Gym API is the whole point of the contribution: any RL codebase that already speaks Gym can point at SoftGym without adapting to a bespoke simulator or reward format.

The suite splits into three tiers. SoftGym-Medium is six tasks with extensive benchmarking results: TransportWater (move a cup without spilling), PourWater (pour a cup of water into a target cup; reward is the fraction of water poured in, not a fixed target amount), StraightenRope (straighten a rope from a random configuration), SpreadCloth (maximize top-down covered area of a crumpled cloth), FoldCloth (fold a flattened cloth in half), and DropCloth (lay a cloth held by two corners flat on the floor via a swing-and-drop motion). SoftGym-Hard adds four harder variants — PourWaterAmount (a specific target volume rather than "as much as possible"), FoldCrumpledCloth, DropFoldCloth, and RopeConfiguration (matching the rope to an arbitrary target shape, including letters of the alphabet, scored by minimum bipartite matching distance between particle positions). SoftGym-Robot swaps the abstract "picker" action space (spheres that can move freely and grip the nearest particle) for a simulated Sawyer or Franka arm with Cartesian end-effector control — though the paper notes this tier "will only be released after obtaining permission from Nvidia."

To isolate where the difficulty in deformable manipulation actually comes from — perception, high-dimensional state, or dynamics itself — the paper benchmarks a deliberately staged set of methods that each assume access to different information:

  • Dynamics Oracle (CEM): the cross-entropy method for planning against the ground-truth particle dynamics and ground-truth positions/velocities directly — no learning at all, just optimization over action sequences via model-predictive control. This is the upper bound: a system with access to information no real robot has.
  • State Oracles (SAC): two variants trained with Soft Actor-Critic. The Full State Oracle takes the raw positions of every particle (padded to a fixed max dimension) as its observation — testing whether a policy can learn directly on the true high-dimensional state without any dynamics model. The Reduced State Oracle instead gets a hand-designed low-dimensional summary (e.g. the four corner positions of a cloth, or 10 keypoints along a rope) — testing whether a smart state abstraction, if it could be perfectly perceived in the real world, would be enough.
  • Image-based methods: CURL-SAC (contrastive representation learning on cropped images), DrQ (data-augmented regularized RL), and PlaNet (a learned latent dynamics model used for planning) — the category that most resembles what a real deployed system would actually have to work with: pixels only, no privileged simulator state.
  • Wu et al. 2020, a prior model-free pick-and-place method with a task-specific action space and cloth-segmentation heuristic, added as an additional comparison on SpreadCloth and FoldCloth only.

All methods train for 106 environment steps (PlaNet for 5×105, due to its higher per-step compute cost) across 5 random seeds, on 800 pre-sampled task variations (held out against 200 evaluation variations — e.g. different cloth sizes, cup sizes, water volumes, initial configurations). Performance at each step is normalized to [0, 1] per task using a per-task lower bound l (the performance of a policy that does nothing) and upper bound u (the task's best achievable performance):

ŝ = s − lu − l // normalized performance ŝ from raw performance s; a policy worse than doing nothing scores below 0
// what they found

The results

The paper's main comparison lives in one figure with no results table — every benchmark comparison among the learned methods (CURL-SAC, DrQ, PlaNet) and the state/reduced-state oracles is reported through learning curves and their relative ordering, not a printed scalar score (the one exception, the Dynamics Oracle's exact per-task finals in Appendix C, is discussed in the critique below). The clearest and most consistent pattern across the six SoftGym-Medium tasks: the Dynamics Oracle sits at or near the top of most panels, described in the text as performing "the best" and being "able to solve most of the tasks" — the paper's own hedge, and a real one: on DropCloth specifically, the image-based DrQ curve and the Reduced State Oracle both climb to match or edge above the Dynamics Oracle's line (0.772) for much of the second half of training — DrQ ends near 0.84, and DropCloth is the only one of the six panels where anything clears the oracle line (visible in Figure 2), and on PourWater, DrQ's curve reaches up to the oracle's line around 0.72M and again near 0.9M steps without clearly exceeding it. Elsewhere the oracle's ceiling holds, and it's unsurprising it's competitive at all — it's handed the ground-truth dynamics model itself — but "most," not "every," is the accurate read of the figure.

Below that ceiling, the ordering the paper draws out is: the Reduced State Oracle performs well specifically where its hand-picked summary actually captures the task — strong on StraightenRope, TransportWater and FoldCloth — but "performs poorly on the tasks which may require more information beyond the reduced state, such as in SpreadCloth, where the positions of the four cloth corners are not sufficient to reason about the configuration of the cloth." That's an important qualifier: this oracle's success is task-dependent on how well its designer chose the abstraction, not a general property of low-dimensional states.

Image-based methods are "far below the optimal performance" on many tasks, "especially true for StraightenRope, SpreadCloth, and FoldCloth" — where the paper reads the flat learning curves as having genuinely plateaued rather than merely needing more training: "even with more training time, performance would still not improve." The comparison specifically to the Reduced State Oracle is narrower than that three-task list, though: the paper says image-based methods have "much worse performance" than the reduced-state oracle "in certain tasks such as FoldCloth or StraightenRope" — SpreadCloth isn't part of that specific claim, and Figure 2 shows why: on SpreadCloth the Reduced State Oracle itself collapses to roughly the same low band (under ~0.2) as the image-based cluster, consistent with the paper's own admission that a crumpled cloth's four-corner reduced state "may require more information beyond" to describe its configuration. On the remaining tasks (TransportWater, PourWater, DropCloth), image-based methods still fall well short of the upper bound of 1, though the gap to the state-based oracles is comparatively smaller there — on DropCloth specifically, DrQ tracks close to both the Reduced State Oracle and the Dynamics Oracle by the end of training. The Full State Oracle — full particle positions fed straight into SAC with no dynamics model — performs poorly on all tasks, which the paper attributes to forcing the network to learn the deformable object's geometric structure implicitly from an unstructured, variable-length position vector, "which adds significantly to the complexity of the learning problem."

On SpreadCloth, adding the prior method from Wu et al. (2020) — which uses a segmentation-guided pick-and-place action space rather than the abstract picker used by everything else — shows it sitting above the other five learned SoftGym methods (Reduced/Full State Oracle, CURL-SAC, DrQ, PlaNet) after roughly the first 0.1M steps — its curve sits inside the same 0.05–0.17 cluster as the others before then — though still well below the Dynamics Oracle's ceiling; the paper attributes the gain over those five to "the use of the segmentation map and a better action space for exploration," not a fundamentally more capable learner, and notes "there still exists a large room for improvement." The same method also "does not perform very well" when carried over to FoldCloth.

Two further, smaller experiments back up the headline story. First, a future-prediction diagnostic: since PlaNet learns its own latent dynamics model, the authors feed it five real frames plus a planned action sequence and visualize what it predicts will happen next.

PlaNet's predicted rollouts visibly fail to capture the spilled water in PourWater and the deforming shape of the cloth in SpreadCloth — direct, qualitative evidence for why a learned dynamics model struggles here: the thing it needs to predict (complex, high-dimensional contact dynamics) is exactly what it can't represent well from pixels. Second, a small sim-to-real check: the authors built a matching real-world cloth setup with a Sawyer arm and Weiss gripper and ran the same pick-and-place action sequences in both simulation and reality.

The paper reports that "the simulated cloth shows similar behaviour to the real one," offered as qualitative support that the FleX-based cloth model and picker abstraction aren't purely a simulation artifact — while explicitly flagging that "direct sim2real transfer of learned policies is still expected to present a challenge," i.e. this is evidence the simulator's dynamics are a reasonable proxy, not evidence that a policy trained in SoftGym would transfer zero-shot to a real robot.

// does it hold up?

The eval read

The most unusual thing about evaluating this paper as an eval is how little of it is numeric for the methods that matter most. Across 18 pages there is no table of final scores and no per-task numeric leaderboard for any learned method — every comparative claim about CURL-SAC, DrQ and PlaNet ("performs the best," "far below," "outperforms the rest") is a qualitative read of curve position in the six-panel Figure 2 (median of only 5 seeds, wide 25th–75th-percentile bands), not a number you can independently recompute or a statistical test you can check. (The paper does print exact scalars in one place, Appendix C's Supplementary Figure 6 — discussed below — but only for the Dynamics Oracle, at three CEM planning horizons per task, not for any of the learned baselines.) That's a real limitation of the benchmark paper even if it isn't a limitation of the benchmark environments themselves — a reader (or a future paper reusing SoftGym) has to eyeball Figure 2 to know how a new method compares to CURL-SAC or DrQ at convergence, and 5 seeds with visibly overlapping percentile bands (e.g. the image-based cluster on PourWater and DropCloth) leaves real room for two methods to be reported as meaningfully different when they aren't.

The baselines themselves are a fair, contemporary-for-2020 spread — CURL and DrQ were both published earlier that same year and represented the state of the art in closing the image-vs-state RL gap on rigid-body control, so testing whether that same trick works for deformable objects (it mostly doesn't) is a legitimate and informative test, not a strawman. But every baseline shares one property the paper is upfront about: all of them train against the ground-truth, simulator-internal reward function, even the image-based ones that only *observe* pixels. The paper explicitly flags this as an unresolved gap: "computing rewards from high-dimensional observations is an additional challenge that is outside the scope of this paper." That means the headline finding — image-based RL struggles on these tasks — is actually a best case for image-based RL: it isolates the control problem from an even harder problem (reward/success estimation from vision) that any real deployment would also have to solve. The gap to a truly image-only, reward-free pipeline is larger than anything shown here.

Contamination isn't really an applicable risk for a from-scratch simulated RL benchmark — there's no pretraining corpus for a policy to have memorized these specific tasks against — but there is a different form of the same worry: benchmark-author bias in task and hyperparameter design. Reward scaling, learning rates, and CEM planning horizons are all tuned per-task-per-method by the authors (Appendix B), which is standard practice for a from-scratch benchmark paper, but means the relative ordering between methods partly reflects how much tuning effort each received, not an inherent ranking. The paper's own Appendix C makes the point concretely: it reports the Dynamics Oracle's final score at three CEM planning horizons per task, and on TransportWater that score swings from 0.95 at the reported horizon (7) to −3.79 at horizon 3 and −4.99 at horizon 10 — a single hyperparameter choice moving the paper's best-performing baseline by nearly six normalized points, with FoldCloth (0.17 → 0.55 → 0.62 across horizons 7/15/21) and DropCloth (0.52 → 0.77 → 0.59) also visibly sensitive. That cuts against a naive cherry-picking reading, though: on SpreadCloth the reported value (0.83, horizon 15) trails horizon 21's 0.87, and on FoldCloth the reported 0.55 trails horizon 21's 0.62 — the authors are not simply reporting whichever horizon looks best. The paper is transparent about the tuning itself (full hyperparameter tables are provided), which is the right mitigation, but it doesn't remove the effect — and there's a loose end in that same appendix worth flagging: the hyperparameter table in Appendix B.1 lists FoldCloth's reported CEM planning horizon as 30, while Supplementary Figure 6's FoldCloth panel tests only 7/15/21 and marks h=15 (0.55) as "the performance that we report in the main paper" — a value well below the ~0.95 the Dynamics Oracle's FoldCloth line actually reaches in Figure 2. FoldCloth is the only one of the six tasks where Figure 6's labeled "reported" bar doesn't line up with Figure 2's black curve; the other five match closely (0.95, 0.88, 1.00, 0.83, 0.77).

The sim-to-real check is honest about being limited — two qualitative matched rollouts on one cloth-manipulation setup, not a quantitative transfer-gap measurement — and the paper doesn't overclaim from it. The real risk for future users of SoftGym is elsewhere: seven of the ten tasks — the rope and cloth tasks — lean on an abstract "picker" action space (a free-floating sphere that grips whatever's nearest), while the three fluid tasks (TransportWater, PourWater, PourWaterAmount) directly actuate the cup instead. That deliberately decouples "high-level planning" from "low-level grasping" — a reasonable scoping choice the paper states outright, but it means most of SoftGym's reported difficulty is about state representation and dynamics, and comparatively little of it is about the actual grasping/contact problem that dominates real deformable-object manipulation in practice. SoftGym-Robot, which would test the harder grasping-inclusive setting, is the one tier the paper says can't yet be released pending Nvidia's permission.

baselines

Fair and current for 2020 (CURL, DrQ and PlaNet were the leading image-based RL methods that same year), staged deliberately from oracle → state → image to isolate where difficulty comes from — a genuinely informative design, not a strawman comparison.

contamination

Not applicable in the pretraining-memorization sense (from-scratch simulated tasks); the analogous risk is per-task/per-method hyperparameter tuning by the benchmark's own authors, which the paper mitigates by publishing full hyperparameter tables but doesn't eliminate.

what's missed

Every baseline, including the image-only ones, trains against the ground-truth simulator reward — the paper says computing reward from observations is explicitly out of scope — so the reported image-based performance is a best case relative to any pipeline that also has to estimate success from pixels. Grasping/contact difficulty is also mostly abstracted away by the picker action space in 7 of the 10 tasks (the three fluid tasks actuate the cup directly instead).

would raise confidence

A numeric results table (final-performance mean ± std per task/method) instead of curve-reading alone; more than 5 seeds given the visibly overlapping percentile bands; a quantitative (not just qualitative) sim-to-real transfer measurement; and release of SoftGym-Robot so the grasping-inclusive tier can actually be benchmarked.

// bottom line

SoftGym correctly diagnoses a real gap — no standard deformable-object RL benchmark existed — and its staged oracle/state/image method design is a genuinely useful way to localize where the difficulty lives (state dimensionality and dynamics, more than task diversity). But as an evaluation artifact, the paper itself under-delivers relative to the environments it introduces: the empirical case for every learned method rests on one figure of noisy 5-seed curves with no accompanying final-score numbers (the paper's only printed scalars, in Appendix C, cover the Dynamics Oracle alone), and the central image-based-RL-struggles finding is measured under a ground-truth-reward assumption that a real deployment wouldn't have.

// takeaways

What to remember

  1. SoftGym is a 10-task, FleX-based simulated benchmark for deformable-object manipulation (cloth, rope, fluid) with a standard OpenAI Gym API — the first shared environment suite for a domain where prior work each used its own incompatible simulator and task variant.
  2. Its central empirical finding is a staged comparison: a ground-truth-dynamics oracle (CEM) sits at or near the top of most tasks (DropCloth is a partial exception, where image-based DrQ closes the gap by the end of training); a hand-designed reduced-state oracle does well only where its abstraction actually captures the task (it fails on SpreadCloth just like the image-based methods); image-based RL (CURL-SAC, DrQ, PlaNet) plateaus well below the state-based oracles specifically on StraightenRope and FoldCloth, and below the dynamics oracle's upper bound more broadly, even given the full 106-step training budget; and a full-particle-state oracle with no dynamics model performs poorly on every task.
  3. There is no results table and no printed final score for any learned method — the quantitative record for CURL-SAC, DrQ, PlaNet and the state oracles is one 6-panel learning-curve figure (5 seeds). The paper's only printed scalars, in an appendix, cover the Dynamics Oracle alone and reveal real tuning sensitivity (a CEM planning-horizon change swings TransportWater's score from 0.95 to −4.99). And every baseline, including the image-only ones, is trained against the ground-truth simulator reward, so the "image-based RL struggles" finding excludes the reward-estimation problem a real robot would also face.
